title: Varying a contract
subtitle: Practical benefit, part-payment and no oral modification clauses
objectives: Explain how 'practical benefit' can supply consideration for a promise to pay MORE for an existing contractual obligation, following Williams v Roffey
State why the same reasoning has not rescued promises to accept LESS, and explain the continuing authority of Foakes v Beer
Assess the effect of a no oral modification clause on a purported variation, applying MWB v Rock Advertising

leadingAuthorities.citation: Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd [1991] 1 QB 1
leadingAuthorities.role: Practical benefit can be good consideration for a promise to pay MORE for existing performance
Part payment of a debt is not good consideration for a promise to accept LESS
Confirms Roffey's practical-benefit reasoning does not extend to part-payment promises

leadingAuthorities.citation: MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd v Rock Advertising Ltd [2018] UKSC 24
leadingAuthorities.role: No oral modification clauses are legally effective; an oral variation made in breach of one is generally invalid

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can state 'consideration is needed to vary a contract' but freeze the moment a fact pattern involves a struggling subcontractor or a landlord under pressure — because the rule genuinely depends on which direction the money is moving. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the definitions — this lesson is about which case governs which direction of change.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the case names here before. The test pool below leans towards application: expect fact patterns that hide whether the variation increases or decreases what's owed, not definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about what Williams v Roffey actually decided — the rest of the lesson depends on you not confusing 'practical benefit' with 'any benefit at all'.

overview.hook: A building site, six weeks from a penalty clause, and a subcontractor who has quietly run out of money. The main contractor doesn't need a new bargain — he needs the old one finished on time. So he promises more money for the same work. Nothing has changed on paper. Everything has changed in law.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. The core case law here (Roffey, Foakes, Selectmove) is long-settled; Rock Advertising (2018) is the most recent addition and remains the leading authority on NOM clauses.

parts.heading: The rule that trapped a struggling contractor
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Start with the old position. In Stilk v Myrick (1809), two sailors deserted mid-voyage; the captain promised the remaining crew extra wages to sail the ship home short-handed. The court refused to enforce the promise — the crew were already contractually bound to do whatever the voyage required, so doing the same job with fewer hands was not fresh consideration for extra pay. Performance of an existing contractual duty, owed to the same party, is not good consideration for a new promise. That was the rule for nearly two centuries.

Then came Williams v Roffey. A building contractor, Roffey Bros, had a contract to refurbish a block of flats and had subcontracted the carpentry to Williams for a fixed price. Williams got into financial difficulty and fell behind — partly because his original price was too low, partly because his supervision was poor. Roffey Bros faced a penalty clause if the main contract overran, so they promised Williams an extra £10,300, paid per flat completed, to finish on time. Williams did more work; Roffey Bros then refused to pay the extra sum, arguing — correctly, on Stilk v Myrick — that Williams was only doing what he was already bound to do.

The Court of Appeal enforced the promise anyway. Williams was still performing his existing duty, so this wasn't a case of doing something new — but the court held that Roffey Bros had received a **practical benefit**: avoiding the penalty clause, avoiding the cost and disruption of finding a new carpenter mid-project, and getting the flats finished to schedule. That benefit, the court said, was capable of being good consideration for the promise to pay more, even though Williams's contractual obligations never changed.

components.caseName: Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd
components.factsShort: A main contractor promised a struggling carpentry subcontractor extra money to finish on time, to avoid a penalty clause and the cost of re-engaging another subcontractor.
components.ratioShort: A practical benefit obtained by the promisor — even without any new legal obligation on the promisee — can be good consideration for a promise to pay more for existing performance.

expanded.facts: Roffey Bros were main contractors on a block of 27 flats and had subcontracted carpentry work to Williams for £20,000. Williams, under-priced from the outset and poorly supervising the job, fell into financial difficulty and was unable to complete on time. Roffey Bros, who would be liable under a penalty clause in the head contract for late completion, and who knew that finding a replacement subcontractor mid-project would be expensive and disruptive, promised Williams an additional £10,300 (£575 per completed flat) to finish the work. Williams carried on and substantially completed eight further flats before Roffey Bros stopped paying the bonus, relying on the fact that Williams was merely doing what his original contract already required.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Glidewell LJ held that where A has entered a contract with B for goods or services in return for payment, and before A has completed performance B has reason to doubt A will complete on time, and B promises A additional payment in return for A's promise to complete on time, and as a result of that promise B obtains in practice a benefit or obviates a disbenefit, and B's promise is not given as a result of economic duress or fraud, then the benefit to B is capable of being good consideration for B's promise — so that the promise is legally binding.
expanded.significance: Roffey narrowed, without overruling, Stilk v Myrick: the old rule survives where a promisee offers nothing beyond existing performance and the promisor gets nothing beyond existing performance in return. But where the promisor extracts a real, practical advantage from making the promise — here, an intact schedule and an intact site team — the law will now find consideration in that advantage. Note precisely what did NOT change: Williams's legal duties under the original contract stayed exactly the same throughout.

interaction.prompt: In Williams v Roffey, did Williams's legal obligations under the original carpentry contract change at any point?
options: No — he remained bound to do exactly what he was already bound to do
Yes — the court implied a new, more demanding contract
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct, and this is the detail that trips people up: Roffey isn't a case about Williams promising something new. The consideration is found entirely in the benefit Roffey Bros received, not in any change to Williams's duties.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again — Williams's duties never changed. That's exactly why this case matters: consideration was found in Roffey Bros's practical benefit, not in any fresh obligation taken on by Williams.

parts.heading: The anatomy of 'practical benefit'
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Glidewell LJ's judgment in Roffey is usually broken down into a checklist, and it rewards being learned precisely, because examiners will test whether you can tell a genuine Roffey scenario from one that merely resembles it.

Two conditions do the most work and are the most commonly mishandled. First, the 'benefit' must be a real, identifiable practical advantage — not simply the abstract fact that the other party is now more likely to perform. Avoiding a penalty clause, avoiding the cost of engaging a replacement, and avoiding disruption to other trades on site were all treated as genuine benefits in Roffey itself; a vague hope that things 'might go more smoothly' would not be enough. Second, and often overlooked, the promise must not be procured by economic duress or fraud — a promisor who is effectively held to ransom by a threat to breach is not bound merely because a 'benefit' can technically be identified.

Keep this doctrine in its lane. It answers one question only: can a promise to pay MORE for the same performance be enforced? It says nothing about promises to accept LESS — that is a different question, with a different (and much older) answer, which the next part deals with.

components.label: Glidewell LJ's conditions for practical benefit consideration
points: A has a contract with B for goods, services or work, for payment by B
Before A has completed performance, B has reason to doubt A will, or can, complete on time or at all
B promises A additional payment (or some other consideration) in return for A's promise to complete on time
As a result of giving that promise, B obtains a practical benefit, or obviates a disbenefit
B's promise is not given as a result of economic duress or fraud on A's part
The benefit to B is capable in law of being good consideration

components.definition: A real, factual advantage obtained by the promisor from making the promise — such as avoiding the cost, delay or disruption of finding a substitute — as distinct from a mere abstract expectation that the other party will now perform. It is capable of amounting to consideration for a promise to pay more, even though it is not a new legal right against the promisee.

interaction.prompt: Put these events from Williams v Roffey in the order they happened.
items: Roffey Bros subcontract the carpentry to Williams for a fixed price
Williams falls behind, risking the penalty clause in the head contract
Roffey Bros promise Williams extra money per flat completed
Williams substantially completes further flats; Roffey Bros stop paying the bonus
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the shape of the case: the promise to pay more comes precisely at the point Roffey Bros faces a real practical loss — which is exactly the moment the 'benefit' the doctrine requires becomes identifiable.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the promise to pay more is made in response to a specific, practical risk to Roffey Bros (the penalty clause and the cost of a replacement), not at the start of the relationship.

parts.heading: Why paying less is different
parts.voice: argumentative — states the tempting extension, then shuts it down
body: Here's the argument a student under exam pressure often reaches for: if a practical benefit can support a promise to pay MORE, surely the same logic supports a promise to accept LESS? A creditor who agrees to take part payment of a debt also gets a practical benefit — getting some money now rather than the risk, cost and delay of chasing all of it later. Why shouldn't that count too?

The law's answer is that it doesn't, and the reason is a much older case than Roffey. In Foakes v Beer (1884), Mrs Beer was owed a debt by Dr Foakes under a judgment. She agreed he could pay it off in instalments, and once he had paid every instalment in full, she then claimed additional interest that had technically accrued on the judgment debt, which her promise had said nothing about excluding. The House of Lords held her entitled to it: an agreement to accept payment of part of a debt, even where the debtor performs exactly as agreed, is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the rest. This restates the much older rule in Pinnel's Case — payment of a lesser sum on the day cannot satisfy a larger obligation, because the debtor is only doing what he already owed.

Roffey did not touch this rule, and Re Selectmove Ltd (1995) confirms it directly. A company owed the Inland Revenue tax arrears and claimed an officer had orally agreed it could pay by instalments; the Revenue later demanded the full sum and petitioned to wind the company up. The company argued Roffey: the Revenue got a practical benefit from an orderly, agreed repayment schedule rather than the uncertainty of enforcement. The Court of Appeal rejected the argument. Practical benefit reasoning, it held, applies to promises to pay MORE, not promises to accept LESS — and extending it to debt cases would effectively overrule Foakes v Beer, which only the House of Lords (now the Supreme Court) could do. Foakes v Beer therefore still stands, subject only to the separate doctrine of promissory estoppel — a genuinely different route to the same kind of result, and the subject of the next lesson.

components.factsShort: A creditor agreed to accept payment of a judgment debt by instalments; the debtor paid in full but the creditor then claimed accrued interest the agreement hadn't mentioned.
components.ratioShort: Payment of part of a debt, however faithfully performed, is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the balance — following Pinnel's Case.

expanded.facts: Dr Foakes owed Mrs Beer a sum under a court judgment. She agreed in writing that if he paid an initial sum and the balance by instalments, she would not take further proceedings on the judgment. Foakes paid every instalment exactly as agreed. Mrs Beer then sued for the statutory interest that had accrued on the judgment debt, which her written agreement had not expressly excluded.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords held that Foakes's performance of the instalment agreement was not good consideration for Mrs Beer's implicit promise not to pursue the interest, because he was doing no more than paying part of what he already owed. Whatever practical convenience the creditor gained from a structured, reliable repayment schedule, the debtor gave nothing in law that he was not already obliged to give.
expanded.significance: This is the debt-side mirror of Stilk v Myrick, and it has never been overruled. It means a creditor who promises to accept less can, in the absence of some fresh element — a different form of payment, an earlier payment date, a third party contributing, or promissory estoppel — go back on that promise and sue for the balance.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say Williams v Roffey 'overruled' or 'got round' Foakes v Beer, since both involve a practical benefit to the party who is asked to give something up.
components.whyItsWrong: Roffey concerns a promise to pay MORE; Foakes v Beer concerns a promise to accept LESS. Re Selectmove makes explicit that practical benefit reasoning is confined to the first situation — extending it to debt cases would require overruling a House of Lords authority, which the Court of Appeal has no power to do. The two lines of authority run in parallel, not in conflict.

interaction.prompt: Which of these promises is capable of being supported by 'practical benefit' consideration alone, without more?
interaction.scenarioA: A client owes a builder £8,000 for finished work; the builder, needing cash quickly, agrees to accept £6,000 in full settlement.
interaction.scenarioB: A client who has contracted a builder for a fixed price offers an extra £2,000 to finish a week early, so the client can complete a property sale on time.
interaction.explanation: B is a promise to pay MORE for performance — the client's practical benefit (an on-time property sale) can support it, following Williams v Roffey. A is a promise to accept LESS of an existing debt — practical benefit reasoning does not rescue it; that remains governed by Foakes v Beer, unless promissory estoppel applies.

parts.heading: Locking in the deal: no oral modification clauses
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the puzzle before resolving it
body: Suppose two commercial parties write into their contract: 'no variation of this agreement shall be effective unless in writing and signed by both parties.' Then, months later, one party's representative has a phone call with the other and they informally agree to change the payment schedule. Is that oral agreement binding, or does the written clause defeat it? Before Rock Advertising, this was genuinely unsettled — some judges reasoned that since the parties were always free to agree anything they liked, they must also be free to agree it orally, whatever their earlier written contract said. A later, purely oral agreement, on this view, could simply override an earlier no oral modification (NOM) clause, because party autonomy cuts both ways.

The Supreme Court resolved the question in MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd v Rock Advertising Ltd (2018). MWB operated serviced offices; Rock Advertising fell behind on licence fees, and its director claimed to have orally agreed a revised, lower payment schedule with an MWB credit controller over the phone. The written licence agreement contained a NOM clause. MWB later locked Rock Advertising out for arrears and sued for the amount due under the original written terms; Rock Advertising counterclaimed, relying on the alleged oral variation.

The Supreme Court held that NOM clauses are legally effective, and an oral variation made in breach of one does not bind the parties. Lord Sumption rejected the 'autonomy cuts both ways' argument: a NOM clause does not restrict the parties' freedom to agree whatever they like — it simply requires that a genuine agreement to vary be recorded in the way they have already, freely, chosen. The commercial value of NOM clauses, he held, lies precisely in preventing disputes about whether an informal exchange amounted to a binding variation, and in creating a reliable record for larger organisations where authority to agree changes may be limited to particular people.

This does not make an oral variation attempted in breach of a NOM clause entirely without consequence. The Supreme Court left open the possibility that the party relying on the oral agreement might, on the right facts, be able to raise an estoppel to prevent the other side from insisting on the writing requirement — but that requires something more than the informal exchange itself, such as clear and unequivocal words or conduct beyond the variation agreement, and reliance that makes it inequitable to insist on the clause. That doctrine is the subject of the next lesson.

components.caseName: MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd v Rock Advertising Ltd
components.factsShort: A licensee fell behind on fees and claimed an oral agreement had varied the payment schedule, despite a written clause requiring all variations to be in writing and signed.
components.ratioShort: No oral modification clauses are legally effective; an oral variation made in breach of one does not bind the parties, subject only to a possible estoppel on exceptional facts.

expanded.facts: Rock Advertising licensed serviced office space from MWB under a written agreement containing a clause that no variation would take effect unless in writing and signed by both parties. Rock Advertising fell into arrears; its director claimed to have reached an oral agreement with an MWB credit controller to revise the payment schedule and spread arrears over a longer period. MWB, relying on the original written terms, locked Rock Advertising out of the premises for continuing arrears and sued for the amount outstanding.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Sumption held that party autonomy is engaged not only in the freedom to make a contract but in the freedom to constrain how future changes to it may be made; a NOM clause is itself an exercise of that autonomy, not a limit on it. The safeguard against injustice, he noted, lies in the law of estoppel, which is flexible enough to prevent unconscionable reliance on a NOM clause in appropriate cases, without undermining the certainty the clause exists to provide.
expanded.significance: Rock Advertising ends a genuine uncertainty in English contract law and strongly favours certainty over informality: parties who want to protect a written contract from casual variation by phone call or email can now do so reliably. For students, the key move is spotting the clause in a problem question fact pattern and recognising that an oral variation alone, without more, will not survive it.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Rock Advertising, highlight the sentence that states the core ratio on NOM clauses.
interaction.passage: The law of contract does not normally impose requirements of form on the parties. But party autonomy operates up to the point at which the contract is made, and after that only to the extent that the contract allows. Where a written contract contains a clause requiring variations to be agreed in writing and signed by both parties, an oral agreement to vary the contract will not be effective, because the parties have already agreed, in that clause, on the only way future changes may validly be made. The safeguard against injustice lies in the flexible doctrine of estoppel.
interaction.ratioSentence: Where a written contract contains a clause requiring variations to be agreed in writing and signed by both parties, an oral agreement to vary the contract will not be effective, because the parties have already agreed, in that clause, on the only way future changes may validly be made.

parts.heading: Putting it together: pay more, pay less, and paper trails
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: Three doctrines, one recurring exam trap. Students who have learned each rule in isolation frequently apply the wrong one under time pressure, because all three fact patterns look superficially alike: two parties, an existing contract, and a proposed change.

The sorting question is always the same, and it should be the first thing you ask: which direction is the money (or the obligation) moving, and is the variation written down where the contract requires it to be? A promise to pay MORE for the same performance turns on Williams v Roffey and practical benefit. A promise to accept LESS of an existing debt turns on Foakes v Beer, unmoved by Selectmove, and unavailable to rescue by practical benefit reasoning — though promissory estoppel may yet apply, on facts covered next. And any variation at all, in either direction, must additionally survive a NOM clause if the original contract contains one, following Rock Advertising — an oral 'yes, that's fine' from the wrong person, however genuine, risks being legally nothing at all.

Get the sorting question right first, and the case law that follows becomes a matter of applying a rule you've already correctly identified — rather than reaching for the first case name that comes to mind.

components.title: Sorting a variation problem
components.description: A decision path for classifying a proposed contract variation and identifying the governing authority.

nodes.label: Does the contract contain a no oral modification (NOM) clause?
Yes → was the variation made in writing, signed as the clause requires?
No → variation is invalid under Rock Advertising, unless estoppel applies
Was the variation made in the required form (or is there no NOM clause)? → check direction of the change
Promise to pay MORE for existing performance → Williams v Roffey: is there a practical benefit, absent duress?
Promise to accept LESS of an existing debt → Foakes v Beer / Re Selectmove: practical benefit does not apply; check promissory estoppel

components.textAlternative: First check whether the contract has a NOM clause. If it does, the variation must be made in the required written, signed form, or it is invalid under Rock Advertising (subject to estoppel). Once form is satisfied (or there is no NOM clause), ask whether the variation increases or decreases what is owed. A promise to pay more is governed by Williams v Roffey's practical benefit test. A promise to accept less is governed by Foakes v Beer and Re Selectmove, unaffected by practical benefit reasoning, though promissory estoppel may apply.

interaction.prompt: A written supply contract contains a NOM clause. The buyer's warehouse manager and the supplier's driver informally agree, at the loading bay, to increase the delivery price by £5 per unit because fuel costs have risen. Nothing is put in writing. Is the price increase binding?
options: No — regardless of practical benefit, the variation was not made in the form the NOM clause requires
Yes — practical benefit from continued deliveries makes any oral increase binding
Yes — because it is a promise to pay more, NOM clauses do not apply to price increases
interaction.explanation: The direction of the variation (more, not less) would matter for consideration under Williams v Roffey, but it is irrelevant to the separate formality question. Rock Advertising applies to ANY variation, in either direction: without the writing and signatures the clause requires, the oral increase does not bind the parties.

testPool.prompt: What kind of benefit did the Court of Appeal in Williams v Roffey hold could amount to consideration for a promise to pay more?
acceptableAnswers: avoiding a penalty and the cost of a replacement
testPool.modelAnswer: A practical benefit — a real, identifiable advantage obtained by the promisor, such as avoiding a penalty clause or the cost and disruption of finding a substitute, even though the promisee's legal obligations did not change.

testPool.prompt: Which case held that part payment of a debt is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the balance?
options: Foakes v Beer
Williams v Roffey Bros

testPool.prompt: What did Re Selectmove decide about the relationship between Williams v Roffey and Foakes v Beer?
options: That Roffey implicitly overruled Foakes v Beer for all debt cases
That practical benefit reasoning from Roffey does not extend to promises to accept less, and Foakes v Beer remains binding
That Foakes v Beer only applies to individuals, not companies
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to think a practical-benefit case must logically swallow the part-payment rule, since a creditor plainly gains a practical benefit from agreed instalments too. Selectmove rejects exactly that extension: only the House of Lords/Supreme Court could overrule Foakes v Beer, and the Court of Appeal in Selectmove declined to treat Roffey as having done so.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows when assessing whether a promise to pay MORE for existing performance is supported by consideration.
items: Identify that the promisee's contractual duties have not changed
Ask whether the promisor obtained a practical benefit, or avoided a disbenefit, from making the promise
Check that the promise was not procured by economic duress or fraud
If both are satisfied, treat the practical benefit as good consideration

testPool.prompt: A NOM clause requires variations to be 'in writing and signed by both parties.' Which of the following would satisfy that requirement under Rock Advertising?
options: An exchange of emails in which both parties' authorised representatives type their names confirming agreed new terms
A recorded phone call in which both parties clearly agree to the new terms
A text message from one party's junior employee saying 'sounds fine to me'
testPool.explanation: The clause requires writing signed by both parties; a typed name in an exchange of emails can satisfy 'signed' depending on the clause's precise wording and the parties' conduct, but an oral recording or an unauthorised, informal message does not meet a writing-and-signature requirement at all.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below from Re Selectmove, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: Counsel for the company argued that the Revenue obtained a practical benefit from the agreed instalment arrangement, in line with Williams v Roffey Bros. That argument cannot succeed here. If Williams v Roffey Bros were applied to a promise to accept less, it would in effect leave the principle in Foakes v Beer without any application, and that is not a step open to this court. Foakes v Beer remains good law and binds promises to accept part payment of a debt.
testPool.ratioSentence: If Williams v Roffey Bros were applied to a promise to accept less, it would in effect leave the principle in Foakes v Beer without any application, and that is not a step open to this court.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is governed by Williams v Roffey rather than Foakes v Beer?
testPool.scenarioA: A tenant owing three months' rent persuades the landlord to accept two months' rent as full settlement of the arrears.
testPool.scenarioB: A caterer, worried a supplier will not deliver in time for a wedding, promises the supplier a bonus to guarantee delivery a day early.
testPool.explanation: B is a promise to pay MORE for performance, governed by Roffey's practical benefit test (the caterer avoids the disruption of a late or missing delivery). A is a promise to accept LESS of an existing debt, governed by Foakes v Beer.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that makes a practical benefit argument available to the promisor in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: A festival organiser has contracted a security firm to provide guards for a weekend event. Ten days before the event, the firm signals it may be short-staffed and unable to fulfil the contract. Worried about losing its licence if security falls short, the organiser promises the firm an extra £3,000 to guarantee full staffing on the day.
testPool.explanation: The practical benefit is the organiser's escape from a genuine risk — losing its licence if security falls short — which is exactly the kind of practical, real-world advantage Roffey requires. The promise of extra money is the consideration itself, not the benefit that supports it.

testPool.prompt: A shopfitter is behind schedule on a fixed-price job. The shop owner, needing the store open for a pre-booked launch event, promises an extra £4,000 to finish in time, with no suggestion of any pressure or threat from the shopfitter. Is the promise supported by consideration?
options: Yes — the owner obtains a practical benefit (an on-time launch) and there is no duress or fraud
No — the shopfitter is only doing what he was already bound to do, so Stilk v Myrick applies without exception
No — practical benefit only applies to construction contracts
testPool.explanation: This is a straightforward Roffey scenario: a promise to pay more, a genuine practical benefit to the promisor, and no duress or fraud. All the conditions in Glidewell LJ's formulation are satisfied.

testPool.prompt: A supplier is owed £15,000 by a struggling retailer. The supplier agrees to accept £11,000 in full and final settlement, purely because it would rather have some money now than risk getting nothing later. The retailer pays the £11,000 in full. Can the supplier still sue for the remaining £4,000?
options: Yes — under Foakes v Beer, part payment of a debt is not good consideration for a promise to accept less, so the promise is not binding on the supplier
No — the supplier obtained a practical benefit (certainty of payment), which is good consideration under Williams v Roffey
No — once the retailer has paid, the debt is automatically extinguished regardless of any promise
testPool.explanation: This is a pure part-payment scenario. Whatever practical benefit the supplier gets from certainty, Re Selectmove confirms that practical benefit reasoning does not rescue a promise to accept less; Foakes v Beer governs, and (absent promissory estoppel, covered next lesson) the supplier remains free to sue for the balance.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that an oral agreement can override a written NOM clause simply because the parties are always free to agree anything they like?
testPool.explanation: Rock Advertising rejected exactly this argument. Party autonomy explains why a NOM clause is enforceable in the first place — the parties chose that formality requirement — not why it can be informally undone; an oral variation made in breach of the clause is invalid, subject only to a possible estoppel on exceptional facts.

testPool.prompt: A written contract for the supply of office furniture contains a clause requiring all variations to be in writing and signed by both parties. Delivery is running late. The buyer's operations manager phones the supplier and orally agrees to pay an extra £1,500 for the supplier to prioritise the order and deliver within 48 hours, since the buyer is opening a new office on a fixed date. The supplier delivers on time and later invoices for the extra £1,500, which the buyer refuses to pay, pointing to the NOM clause. Analyse whether the extra £1,500 is recoverable.
factsToOrder: The contract contains a NOM clause requiring written, signed variations
The variation (the promise of extra payment) was made orally, by phone
The buyer obtains a practical benefit: opening the new office on the fixed date
The buyer later refuses to pay, relying on the NOM clause

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the oral promise to pay an extra £1,500, made in breach of the contract's NOM clause, is legally binding.
modelAnswer.rule: Even where a promise to pay more for existing performance would otherwise be supported by practical benefit consideration under Williams v Roffey, a variation made in breach of a valid no oral modification clause is not effective, following MWB v Rock Advertising, unless an estoppel can be raised on the facts.
modelAnswer.application: The practical benefit point is satisfied here — the buyer avoided the disruption of a delayed office opening, so consideration would not be the obstacle if this were assessed purely as a Roffey problem. But the contract contains a NOM clause requiring written, signed variations, and the extra payment was agreed only by phone. Rock Advertising treats that formality requirement as decisive: an oral variation in breach of the clause does not bind the parties, regardless of consideration.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The £1,500 is not recoverable as a matter of contractual variation; the oral agreement, however genuine, fails for want of the form the NOM clause requires.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures why Williams v Roffey did not overrule Stilk v Myrick?
options: Stilk v Myrick has since been fully abolished as a rule of English law
Roffey narrowed Stilk v Myrick's application without overruling it: where the promisor gains no identifiable practical benefit, performance of an existing duty is still not good consideration
Stilk v Myrick only ever applied to maritime contracts
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to treat Roffey as having swept Stilk v Myrick away entirely. It hasn't: where there is no real, identifiable practical benefit to the promisor — just a bare promise to do what was always required — the old rule still bites and the promise to pay more remains unenforceable for want of consideration.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying Williams v Roffey to a promise to accept LESS, or applying Foakes v Beer to a promise to pay MORE. Before reaching for a case name, always ask first which direction the money is moving — and separately, whether a NOM clause governs the form the variation must take.
